facts.quote: The steel fabrication company, August Klönne supplied 17,000 tonnes (37,000,000 lb) of steel for the structure of the platform halls and the masonry consists of Elbe Sandstone.

facts.fact: The whole station went into operation on 16 April 1898.
facts.quote: After more than five years of construction the whole building went into operation  on 16 April 1898.

facts.fact: In the early-21st-century restoration the train sheds were roofed with translucent Teflon-coated glass-fibre membranes that let in more daylight.
facts.quote: The building is notable for its train-sheds, which are roofed with Teflon-coated glass fibre membranes. This translucent roof design, installed during the comprehensive restoration of the station at the beginning of the 21st century, allows more daylight to reach the concourses than was previously possible.

facts.fact: The 34-metre dome over the connecting hall and the large waiting rooms were restored to their historic design.
facts.quote: The dome above the connection hall between the two halls, which is up to 34 metres (111 ft 7 in) high, the connecting hall and the large waiting rooms were restored to their historical designs.

facts.fact: The station was heritage-listed in 1978.
facts.quote: In 1978, the Dresden Hauptbahnhof was heritage-listed.

facts.fact: The Robert C. Weaver Federal Building is a ten-storey office building in Washington, D.C., built as the headquarters of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
facts.quote: The Robert C. Weaver Federal Building is a ten-story office building in Washington, D.C., United States. Owned by the U.S. federal government, it was built by the General Services Administration as the headquarters of the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

facts.fact: Marcel Breuer designed it in the brutalist style, and it was completed in 1968; it is on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: Designed by Marcel Breuer in the brutalist style, it was completed in 1968. The building is one of two that Breuer designed for the U.S. federal government in the District of Columbia, along with the Hubert H. Humphrey Building, and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: Its curving precast concrete facade is like Breuer's earlier UNESCO Headquarters and IBM La Gaude.
facts.quote: The Weaver Building has a curvilinear precast concrete facade, similar to Breuer's previous UNESCO Headquarters and IBM La Gaude.

facts.fact: In plan it is two back-to-back Ys, with four curving wings off a long core.
facts.quote: It is shaped like two back-to-back "Y"s, with four curving wings extending off an elongated core.

facts.fact: Concrete panels hold deeply recessed rectangular windows, and the ground floor is set back behind concrete pilotis.
facts.quote: The facade contains concrete panels with deeply recessed rectangular windows; the ground floor is recessed behind concrete pilotis.

facts.fact: Breuer designed a 6-acre plaza that is also the roof of an underground car park.
facts.quote: Breuer designed a 6-acre (2.4 ha) plaza, which serves as the roof for an underground parking garage.

facts.fact: Concrete was chosen because it symbolised "enterprise and vigor", two of Kennedy's Guiding Principles for federal buildings.
facts.quote: The material was used because it symbolized "enterprise and vigor", two of Kennedy's Guiding Principles.

facts.fact: Its design was praised when built, but its brutalism has also drawn criticism, especially from several HUD secretaries.
facts.quote: Although the building's design received architectural praise when it was built, its brutalist style and the unoriginality of its design have also received negative commentary, especially from several HUD secretaries.

facts.fact: The CCCB is an arts centre in Barcelona's Raval district whose core theme is the city and urban culture.
facts.quote: The Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona (also known by its acronym, CCCB) is an arts centre in Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the Raval district, the centre's core theme is the city and urban culture.

facts.fact: It occupies part of the old Casa de Caritat almshouse, built in 1802 and used as an almshouse until 1957.
facts.quote: The CCCB occupies part of the old Casa de Caritat almshouse, built in 1802 and serving this role until 1957.

facts.fact: The remodelling is the work of Helio Piñón and Albert Viaplana and won the FAD and Ciutat de Barcelona Architecture Prizes in 1993.
facts.quote: The remodelled premises are the work of the architects Helio Piñón and Albert Viaplana, and, in 1993, the project was awarded the FAD and Ciutat de Barcelona Architecture Prizes.

facts.fact: The new building replaced the north wing, completing the U-shaped plan with a 30-metre-high prism whose glazed façade leans out over the courtyard at the top.
facts.quote: The new project replaced the north wing, completing the original U-shaped layout with a 30-metre-high prismatic volume, presenting a spectacular glazed façade that projects into the courtyard at the top.

facts.fact: The glass façade reflects the surrounding rooftops, works as a lookout over the city and holds the halls, lifts and stairs.
facts.quote: With its interplay of reflections, this new feature becomes a mirror of the surrounding rooftops and a prime lookout point over the city, as well as housing internal communications (halls, lifts and stairs).

facts.fact: The centre has 15,000 m² of floor space, 4,000 m² of it for exhibitions.
facts.quote: The centre has a floor area of 15,000 m2, of which 4,000 are exhibition spaces.

facts.fact: In 2011 the centre took in the former Casa de Caritat theatre, built in 1912 by Josep Goday i Casals, through a project by Martínez Lapeña-Torres.
facts.quote: The project, designed by Martinez Lapeña-Torres Arquitectos, SL, forms a basement-level connection with the current premises, in the Pati de les Dones courtyard, and addresses the old theatre, built in 1912 by the architect Josep Goday i Casals, and part of one of the 19th-century cloisters of the former Hospital de la Caritat.

facts.fact: Messe Torhaus is a high-rise in Frankfurt's Bockenheim district, designed by Oswald Mathias Ungers.
facts.quote: Messe Torhaus is a high-rise building in the Bockenheim district of Frankfurt, Germany. It was designed by Oswald Mathias Ungers.

facts.fact: Hochtief built the 60,000-tonne building with 400 workers in a record 13 months, from 1983 to 1984.
facts.quote: Built by Hochtief, 400 workers constructed the 60,000 ton building in a record time of 13 months from 1983 to 1984.

facts.fact: Its unusual shape and materials are said to resemble a guillotine.
facts.quote: Its unusual shape and use of materials resembles a guillotine.

facts.fact: It houses the administration of Messe Frankfurt, along with services such as a kindergarten and the press centre.
facts.quote: The building houses the administration of Messe Frankfurt as well as services like a kindergarten and the press centre.

facts.fact: The tower is 117 m high with 30 floors.
facts.quote: It is 117 m high and has 30 floors.

facts.fact: A nearby power plant uses the gatehouse as its chimney, so the building is also called "Frankfurt's most beautiful fireplace".
facts.quote: In the immediate vicinity is located on the fairgrounds of Messe Frankfurt, the CHP Mainova AG, which serves as a gate house chimney. Therefore, the building is also known as "Frankfurt's most beautiful fireplace".

facts.fact: Ungers's work on the Frankfurt Messe grounds was often described as a "new clarity".
facts.quote: In connection with his construction on the Frankfurt Messe grounds, there was often talk of a "new clarity".

facts.fact: Bodegas Güell is a winery complex in Garraf, Sitges, designed by Antoni Gaudí.
facts.quote: Bodegas Güell, in Catalan Celler Güell, is an architectural complex comprising a winery and associated buildings located in Garraf, in the Spanish municipality of Sitges (Barcelona), designed by the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí.

facts.fact: Gaudí's patron Eusebi Güell commissioned the work in 1882.
facts.quote: Gaudí received the commission for this work in 1882 from his patron Eusebi Güell, who had seen Gaudí's work at the Paris Expo in 1878; in this year Gaudí received a number of other commissions including the Palau Güell, the Pavellons Güell in Pedralbes, the Park Güell and the crypt of the Church of Colònia Güell in Santa Coloma de Cervelló.

facts.fact: The original commission included hunting pavilions as well as the winery, but they were never built.
facts.quote: The original commission consisted of the winery and several hunting pavilions, but the latter were never built.

facts.fact: The winery was built between 1895 and 1897 under the direction of Gaudí's assistant Francesc Berenguer.
facts.quote: The winery buildings were finally built between 1895 and 1897, under the direction of Francesc Berenguer, Gaudí's assistant.

facts.fact: The winery has a triangular front profile with almost vertical roofs of steeply sloping stone slabs, topped by chimneys.
facts.quote: The winery has a triangular frontal profile, with almost vertical roofs, steep sloping stone slabs, finished off with sets of chimneys and two doors that connect it to the old building.

facts.fact: It has three floors: vehicle parking on the ground floor, an apartment on the first and a domed chapel at the top.
facts.quote: There are three floors: the ground floor for parking vehicles, an apartment on the first floor and a domed chapel on the top floor.

facts.fact: Wine was made there until 1936, when production stopped for lack of commercial success; the building now holds a restaurant.
facts.quote: However, production stopped in 1936 due to lack of commercial success. There is currently a restaurant in the Bodegas Güell.

facts.fact: The convention centre officially opened on 4 December 2011.
facts.quote: QNCC was officially opened on 4 December 2011.

facts.fact: Arata Isozaki designed it with RHWL Architects.
facts.quote: Designed by Arata Isozaki in partnership with RHWL Architects, the building is designed to operate efficiently with innovations such as water conservation and energy-efficient fixtures, and it is approximately 32 percent more efficient compared with a similarly designed building that lack such innovations.

facts.fact: It was built to the LEED gold standard of the U.S. Green Building Council.
facts.quote: It was the first of its kind being built to the gold certification standard of the U.S. Green Building Council’s Leadership in Energy and Environment Design (LEED).

facts.fact: 3,500 m² of solar panels provide 12.5 percent of the centre's energy.
facts.quote: One of the features is the 3,500 sqm of solar panels providing 12.5 percent of the Centre's energy needs.

facts.fact: The columns at the front represent the Sidrat al-Muntaha, a sacred tree in Islam.
facts.quote: The columns at the front of the building to symbolise a Sidrat al-Muntaha, a sacred Islamic tree believed to mark the end of the seventh heaven in the Islamic religion.

facts.fact: It has a 4,000-seat conference hall, a 2,300-seat theatre, three auditoria and 52 meeting rooms.
facts.quote: QNCC features a conference hall of 4,000 seats theatre style, a 2,300-seat theatre, three auditoria and a total of 52 flexible meetings rooms to accommodate a wide range of events.

facts.fact: The venue covers 200,000 m², including 40,000 m² of exhibition space over nine halls.
facts.quote: It has 200,000 square metres of venue area, which includes 40,000 square metres of exhibition space over nine halls, and is adaptable to seat 10,000 for a conference or banquet.

facts.fact: Hospicio Cabañas in Guadalajara was one of the oldest and largest orphanage and hospital complexes in the Americas, and is now a museum.
facts.quote: The Hospicio Cabañas (Spanish pronunciation: [osˈpisjo kaˈβaɲas]) or Cabañas Museum in Guadalajara, Jalisco was one of the oldest and largest orphanage and hospital complexes in the Americas.

facts.fact: It was founded in 1810 to combine a workhouse, hospital, orphanage and almshouse.
facts.quote: The complex was founded in 1810 by the Bishop of Guadalajara in order to combine the functions of a workhouse, hospital, orphanage, and almshouse.

facts.fact: Bishop Juan Ruiz de Cabañas engaged the Mexico City architect Manuel Tolsá, whose design drew on Les Invalides in Paris and El Escorial.
facts.quote: It owes its name to Juan Ruiz de Cabañas who was appointed to the see of Guadalajara in 1796 and engaged Manuel Tolsá, a renowned architect from Mexico City, to design the structure. Tolsá's design was based on classic examples such as Les Invalides in Paris and El Escorial near Madrid.

facts.fact: The single-storey buildings form a 164 by 145 metre rectangle and are 7.5 metres high.
facts.quote: The buildings form a rectangle measuring 164 by 145 metres (538 by 476 ft). These are single-storey structures which are 7.5 metres (25 ft) in height.

facts.fact: The chapel is twice as high as the rest and has a dome rising to 32.5 metres.
facts.quote: The chapel is twice as high and has a dome rising to 32.5 metres (107 ft).

facts.fact: The complex was built on one level to make it easier for the sick, the old and children to move around.
facts.quote: The complex is erected on one level, "so as to facilitate the movement of the sick, the aged, and children."

facts.fact: The interior's highlight is José Clemente Orozco's fresco cycle, including The Man of Fire (1936–39).
facts.quote: The highlight of the interior decoration is a series of monumental frescoes by José Clemente Orozco, including one of his most famed creations, the allegory of The Man of Fire (1936–39).

facts.fact: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
facts.quote: Hospicio Cabañas was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

facts.fact: The Ananda Temple in Bagan is a Buddhist temple built in 1105 under King Kyansittha of the Pagan Dynasty.
facts.quote: The Ananda Temple (Burmese: အာနန္ဒာ ဘုရား, pronounced [ànàɰ̃dà pʰəjá]), located in Bagan, Myanmar is a Buddhist temple built in 1105 AD during the reign (1084–1112/13) of King Kyansittha (Hti-Hlaing Min) of the Pagan Dynasty.

facts.fact: Its cruciform plan rises in terraces to a small pagoda topped by a hti umbrella.
facts.quote: The temple layout is cruciform with several terraces leading to a small pagoda at the top covered by an umbrella known as hti, which is the name of the umbrella or top ornament found in almost all pagodas in Myanmar.

facts.fact: Four standing Buddha statues face east, north, west and south.
facts.quote: The Buddhist temple houses four standing Buddha statues, each one facing the cardinal direction of East, North, West and South.

facts.fact: The temple fuses Mon architecture with an adopted Indian style.
facts.quote: The temple is said to be an architectural wonder in a fusion of Mon and adopted Indian style of architecture.

facts.fact: It is built of brick and plaster, with stone images and glazed terracotta plaques meant to teach Theravada Buddhism.
facts.quote: It has been built with bricks and plaster depicting iconographic images in stones and plaques (terra-cotta glazed tiles) with the main purpose of educating the people of the region in the religious ethos of Theravada Buddhism and in accordance with the personal beliefs of the King Kyansittha.

facts.fact: The central square is 53 metres across, with gabled porches projecting 17 metres from each face.
facts.quote: It has a central square of 53 metres (174 ft); gabled porches project out by 57 feet (17 m) from each face of the square. The superstructure is 51 metres (167 ft) in height formed by decorated terraces.

facts.fact: Jataka scenes of the Buddha's life are shown on 554 terracotta tiles around the base, sides and terraces.
facts.quote: Jataka scenes (life story of the Buddha – said to be sourced from Mon texts) are embossed over 554 terra cotta tiles that decorate the base, sides and terraces.

facts.fact: The temple was damaged in the 1975 earthquake and has since been fully restored.
facts.quote: The temple was damaged in the earthquake of 1975. However, it has been fully restored and is well maintained by frequent painting and whitewashing of the walls.

facts.fact: The Navoi Theater is Tashkent's national opera house, built as one of the first modern theatres in the region.
facts.quote: The Navoi Theater, officially the Alisher Navoi State Academic Grand Theatre, is a national opera theater in central Tashkent, built as one of the first modern theaters in the region.

facts.fact: Alexey Shchusev designed it, and it was built in 1942–1947, partly with forced labour.
facts.quote: Designed by Alexey Shchusev, the theater was built in 1942-1947, in part with forced labor.

facts.fact: It opened in November 1947, marking the 500th anniversary of the poet Alisher Navoi's birth.
facts.quote: It opened to the public in November, 1947, celebrating the 500th anniversary of the birth of Alisher Navoi, the greatest representative of Chagatai literature.

facts.fact: The theatre seats 1,400 and its main stage covers 540 m².
facts.quote: The theater has a capacity of 1,400 spectators. The main stage covers 540 square meters.

facts.fact: Japanese prisoners of war worked on its construction from 1945 to 1947.
facts.quote: From 1945 to 1947 Japanese prisoners of war captured by the Soviet Union participated in the building construction under forced labor.

facts.fact: In 1996 a plaque was put up honouring the Japanese workers who helped build it.
facts.quote: In 1996, under then Uzbekistan President Islam Karimov a plaque was installed at the theater honoring the Japanese workers involved in its construction.

facts.fact: The library in the ECLAC building in Santiago is named after the diplomat Hernán Santa Cruz.
facts.quote: In honor of his work creating ECLAC and his work in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the library in the ECLAC building in Santiago is named after him.

facts.fact: The pilgrimage church Maria, Königin des Friedens in Neviges was designed by Gottfried Böhm and consecrated in 1968.
facts.quote: The principal pilgrimage church Maria, Königin des Friedens, consecrated in 1968, was designed by Gottfried Böhm.

facts.fact: It serves a Catholic pilgrimage to an image of the Immaculate Conception venerated there since 1681.
facts.quote: The veneration of a miraculous image of the Immaculate Conception dates back to 1681.

facts.fact: It was built from 1966 to 1968, while Cardinal Josef Frings was Archbishop of Cologne.
facts.quote: During his time as Archbishop of Cologne, the pilgrimage church Maria, Königin des Friedens was built from 1966 to 1968 according to a design by the architect Gottfried Böhm, who died in 2021.

facts.fact: The Neviges church is Böhm's most influential and recognised building.
facts.quote: Böhm's most influential and recognized building is the Maria, Königin des Friedens pilgrimage church in Neviges.

facts.fact: In 1986 Böhm became the first German architect to win the Pritzker Prize.
facts.quote: In 1986, he became the first German architect to be awarded the prestigious Pritzker Prize.

facts.fact: Cardinal Karol Wojtyła visited the church, known as the "Mariendom", in 1978, weeks before he became Pope John Paul II.
facts.quote: Cardinal Karol Wojtyła visited the "Mariendom" on 23 September 1978 with the German and Polish bishops under the leadership of Primate Cardinal [[Stefan Wyszyński |Wyszyński]] and Cardinal Höffner, 23 days before Wojtyła was elected Pope John Paul II.

facts.fact: Villa Méditerranée in Marseille's 2nd arrondissement was designed by Stefano Boeri as part of the Euroméditerranée urban renewal project.
facts.quote: The Villa Méditerranée (French pronunciation: [vila meditɛʁane]; lit. 'Mediterranean Villa') is a building in the 2nd arrondissement of Marseille, France, designed by Stefano Boeri as part of the Euroméditerranée urban renewal project.

facts.fact: It stands in La Joliette next to MuCEM and opened in 2013 as a conference centre during Marseille-Provence 2013.
facts.quote: It is in the La Joliette neighbourhood just next to the Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations (MuCEM) and opened in 2013 initially as a conference centre amid the Marseille-Provence 2013 celebrations.

facts.fact: The Cinerama Dome on Sunset Boulevard, Hollywood, opened on 7 November 1963 to show widescreen Cinerama films.
facts.quote: Designed to exhibit widescreen Cinerama films, it opened November 7, 1963.

facts.fact: The design was proposed by Pierre Cabrol, lead designer at Welton Becket and Associates, who had worked with R. Buckminster Fuller while studying at MIT.
facts.quote: The design was proposed by French architect Pierre Cabrol, lead designer in the noted architectural firm of Welton Becket and Associates. Pierre Cabrol worked with R. Buckminster Fuller during his studies at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

facts.fact: Working around the clock, the whole construction took only 16 weeks.
facts.quote: Working around the clock, the entire construction spanned only 16 weeks.

facts.fact: It is the only concrete geodesic dome in the world, made of 316 hexagonal and pentagonal panels in 16 sizes.
facts.quote: The Cinerama Dome is the only concrete geodesic dome in the world. The theatre is made up of 316 individual hexagonal and pentagonal shapes in 16 different sizes.

facts.fact: Each panel is about 12 feet across and weighs around 7,500 pounds.
facts.quote: Each of these pieces is approximately 12 feet (3.7 metres) across and weighs around 7,500 pounds (3,400 kilograms).

facts.fact: At opening it had the world's largest contoured cinema screen, 32 by 86 feet.
facts.quote: The theatre also has design elements such as a loge section with stadium seating, architecturally significant floating stairways, and, at the time of its opening, the largest contoured motion-picture screen in the world, measuring 32 ft (9.8 m) high and 86 ft (26 m) wide, with a maximum aspect ratio of 2.69:1.

facts.fact: It was declared a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1998.
facts.quote: The Cinerama Dome was declared a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1998.

facts.fact: Benaroya Hall is the home of the Seattle Symphony, with a 2,500-seat auditorium and a 536-seat recital hall.
facts.quote: It features two auditoria, the S. Mark Taper Foundation Auditorium, a 2,500-seat performance venue, as well as the Illsley Ball Nordstrom Recital Hall, which seats 536.

facts.fact: It opened in September 1998, cost $120 million and is noted for acoustics designed by Cyril Harris.
facts.quote: Opened in September 1998 at a cost of $120 million, Benaroya is noted for its technology-infused acoustics designed by Cyril Harris.

facts.fact: It occupies an entire city block in central Seattle.
facts.quote: Benaroya occupies an entire city block in the center of the city and has helped double the Seattle Symphony's budget and number of performances.

facts.fact: LMN Architects designed it, and it won an AIA National Honor Award in 2001.
facts.quote: The hall was designed by LMN Architects of Seattle, and was awarded the National Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects in 2001.

facts.fact: It sits directly above a rail tunnel, next to the transit tunnel, whose Symphony station is built into the building.
facts.quote: The building sits directly above the Great Northern Tunnel, which carries the primary rail corridor through the city, and adjacent to the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel. The latter has Symphony station, which is directly integrated into the building and was renamed in August 2024 for the Seattle Symphony.

facts.fact: The performance hall floats on rubber pads that isolate it from the outer shell.
facts.quote: The performance hall is insulated by floating on rubber pads which insulate it from the outer shell of the building.

facts.fact: The lobby holds glass art, including Dale Chihuly's Crystal Cascade.
facts.quote: The lobby of the hall features a large contribution of glass art, such as one given the title Crystal Cascade, by artist Dale Chihuly.

facts.fact: The Toronto Reference Library in Yorkville is the largest public reference library in Canada.
facts.quote: The library is the largest public reference library in Canada, with an extensive collection of books, manuscripts, microfilm, and other items.

facts.fact: The new building opened on 2 November 1977, after construction began in 1974.
facts.quote: Construction for the new building began in 1974, with the new building being opened to the public on Asquith Avenue and Yonge Street on 2 November 1977.

facts.fact: Revised designs approved in April 1974 made the building slightly smaller and lower, reduced its massing and changed its cladding to brick.
facts.quote: After several months of consultation with the local government, revised designs were approved in April 1974; which slightly reduced the size and height of the building, reduced its massing, and changed its cladding to brick.

facts.fact: The upper levels step back from the street in a pyramid shape to reduce the building's massing.
facts.quote: The other levels of the building are pushed further back into the property, away from the street; forming a pyramid shape to decrease the massing of the building.

facts.fact: It is built of reinforced concrete, clad in orange-red brick to match the area.
facts.quote: The building was primarily built out of steel reinforced concrete and is clad with orange-reddish brick to match the building material of the other buildings in the area; although glass portions on the sections of the building facing Yonge Street also exists.

facts.fact: A heat pump system recovers heat from lights, visitors and sunlight to regulate the climate inside.
facts.quote: The building climate is regulated through an internal heat pump system that recovers the heat from its lights, visitors, and the solar radiation that passes through the window.

facts.fact: The curved central atrium has a skylight, with plants and water features inspired by the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
facts.quote: The open-space curved central atrium features a skylight and is also designed to allow air to circulate freely. Spread throughout the central atrium are plant and water features, inspired by the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

facts.fact: A 2009–2014 renovation added a glass cube holding an expanded lobby; its design recalls Moriyama's 1973 proposal.
facts.quote: Renovations were undertaken from 2009 to 2014, which saw the building expanded to its present size with a transparent glass cube built onto the structure; the glass cube holds an expanded lobby that includes a shop and café. The design of the cube is reminiscent of the original proposal submitted by Moriyama in 1973.

facts.fact: The Cinquantenaire Arcade is a memorial arcade in Brussels' Parc du Cinquantenaire, centred on a triple arch topped by a bronze quadriga.
facts.quote: The centrepiece is a monumental triple arch known as the Cinquantenaire Arch (French: Arc du Cinquantenaire; Dutch: Triomfboog van het Jubelpark). It is topped by a bronze quadriga sculptural group with a female charioteer, representing the Province of Brabant personified raising the national flag.

facts.fact: It began as part of the 1880 National Exhibition marking 50 years since the Belgian Revolution.
facts.quote: The Cinquantenaire Arcade was part of a project commissioned by the Belgian government under the patronage of King Leopold II for the 1880 National Exhibition, commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Belgian Revolution.

facts.fact: Gédéon Bordiau conceived a single arch; after his death in 1904, Charles Girault redesigned it as a triple arch.
facts.quote: The original single arch of the 1880 exhibition was conceived by the architect Gédéon Bordiau, but upon his death in 1904, the arch's design was revised by the French architect Charles Girault, chosen by Leopold II. Girault designed a triple arch, but preserved Bordiau's idea of the quadriga.

facts.fact: Leopold II inaugurated it on 27 September 1905, for the 75th anniversary of independence.
facts.quote: The basic construction was completed with private funding in May of the same year and the arcade was inaugurated by Leopold II on 27 September 1905, just in time for the 75th anniversary of Belgian independence.

facts.fact: The arch is 30 metres wide and 45 metres high, with three equal bays.
facts.quote: The Cinquantenaire Arch, 30-metre-wide (98 ft) and 45-metre-high (148 ft), has three bays of equal dimensions.

facts.fact: The quadriga, Brabant Raising the National Flag, is by Thomas Vinçotte, with horses by Jules Lagae.
facts.quote: The arch's bronze quadriga, entitled Brabant Raising the National Flag, was made by Thomas Vinçotte and the horses by Jules Lagae.

facts.fact: From 1912 the colonnade's new rear wall was decorated with a 360 m² mosaic frieze by Jean Delville.
facts.quote: The originally open colonnade was closed at the rear by a wall in 1905, which starting in 1912, was decorated with a 360 m2 (3,900 sq ft) mosaic frieze with the theme The glorification of peaceful and heroic Belgium, by Jean Delville.

facts.fact: The monument was protected on 29 June 1984.
facts.quote: The monument received protected status on 29 June 1984.

facts.fact: The CEC Palace on Calea Victoriei in Bucharest, built 1897–1900, is the headquarters of CEC Bank.
facts.quote: The CEC Palace (Romanian: Palatul CEC) in Bucharest, Romania, built between 8 June 1897 and 1900, and situated on Calea Victoriei opposite the National Museum of Romanian History, is the headquarters of CEC Bank.

facts.fact: The land and building were paid for with the bank's own funds.
facts.quote: The land was bought and the building constructed with the institution's own funds.

facts.fact: The site was once occupied by the ruins of a monastery and an inn.
facts.quote: Before the construction of the palace, the location was occupied by the ruins of a monastery (Saint John the Great) and an adjoining inn.

facts.fact: Paul Gottereau, a graduate of the École des Beaux-Arts, designed it, and Ion Socolescu supervised construction.
facts.quote: The project was designed by the architect Paul Gottereau, a graduate of the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris; construction was supervised by the Romanian architect Ion Socolescu.

facts.fact: Built in an eclectic style, it is topped by a glass and metal dome.
facts.quote: Built in eclectic style, the palace is topped by a glass and metal dome.

facts.fact: The entrance arch rests on two pairs of composite columns, and the corners end in gables, coats of arms and Renaissance domes.
facts.quote: The entrance features an arch supported by two pairs of columns in composite style. The four corners are decorated with gables and coats of arms and ending in Renaissance domes.

facts.fact: The Administrative Palace in Satu Mare is 97 metres high, the tallest building in Transylvania.
facts.quote: At 97 metres, it is the highest building in Transylvania and one of the highest in the country.

facts.fact: It is an example of Brutalist architecture.
facts.quote: It is an example of brutalist style architecture.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1972 under chief architect Nicolae Porumbescu, assisted by Ludovic Gyüre.
facts.quote: Thus, in 1972, construction of the building began, the main architect being Nicolae Porumbescu of Iaşi, assisted by Ludovic Gyüre of Satu Mare.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1984 by over 1,000 workers.
facts.quote: The building was completed in 1984; there were over 1,000 workers employed on the project.

facts.fact: It has one main tower and three smaller towers.
facts.quote: The building has three smaller towers and one big main tower.

facts.fact: The three small towers stood for the county's Romanians, Germans and Hungarians, and the main tower for the bond between them.
facts.quote: The three small towers were meant to represent the three ethnic groups present in Satu Mare County: Romanians, Germans and Hungarians, while the main tower represented the bond between these three ethnic groups.

facts.fact: It houses the county council, prefecture, city hall and culture office.
facts.quote: Today, the building houses several government institutions, including the county council, prefecture, city hall and culture office.

facts.fact: The Haludovo Palace Hotel, on the island of Krk, was the centre of a resort designed by Boris Magaš and built from 1969 to 1972.
facts.quote: It formed the architectural and social centre of Haludovo, a large tourist resort designed by Croatian architect Boris Magaš and constructed between 1969 and 1972 during the rapid expansion of tourism on the Yugoslav Adriatic.

facts.fact: The 25-hectare resort was conceived as a self-contained tourist settlement, not a single hotel.
facts.quote: Covering approximately 25 hectares (62 acres), Haludovo was conceived as a self-contained tourist settlement rather than a single hotel.

facts.fact: Its plan referred to a historic city: the Palace as castle, perimeter blocks as city walls and atrium villas as an inner settlement.
facts.quote: The Palace occupied the dominant position of a palace or castle, while linear accommodation buildings at the perimeter suggested city walls and groups of smaller atrium villas formed an interior settlement.

facts.fact: The Palace's communal areas surround a large double-height atrium with a gallery.
facts.quote: The main communal area was organised around a large double-height internal atrium surrounded by a gallery.

facts.fact: Tall, slender concrete columns in the atrium branch into arches at the top.
facts.quote: One of the most distinctive elements of the atrium was a system of tall, slender reinforced-concrete columns whose upper sections branched into arches.

facts.fact: Concrete forms recur across the complex as pergolas, sunshades and roof elements, a repeated motif.
facts.quote: Related concrete forms were repeated throughout the complex as pergolas, sun-shading structures and roof elements, creating a recurring architectural motif.

facts.fact: In 1972 Penthouse founder Bob Guccione set up the Penthouse Adriatic Club, with a casino, in the Palace.
facts.quote: Guccione established the Penthouse Adriatic Club within the Palace, including a casino intended primarily for foreign visitors.

facts.fact: Historians count Haludovo among Magaš's most significant works and an important example of Yugoslav tourist architecture.
facts.quote: Architectural historians regard Haludovo as one of Magaš's most significant works and an important example of Yugoslav tourist architecture.

facts.fact: Sofia Central Station is the main passenger station of Bulgaria's capital and the largest in the country.
facts.quote: The Sofia Central Railway Station (Bulgarian: Централна железопътна гара София, romanized: Tsentralna zhelezopatna gara Sofiya) is the main passenger railway station of Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, as well as the largest railway station in the country.

facts.fact: The new terminal was designed by Transproekt under lead architect Milko Bechev.
facts.quote: The new terminal was designed by the Transproekt company under lead architect Milko Bechev.

facts.fact: It has 365 rooms over two underground and three above-ground levels, with heavy use of white marble.
facts.quote: It included 365 premises placed around two underground and three overground levels. The building made heavy use of white marble.

facts.fact: It was built on the old station's plaza and garden so that trains could keep running during construction.
facts.quote: The new building was constructed in the place of the 1888 station's plaza and garden areas, in order not to interrupt its operations during the construction efforts.

facts.fact: Construction of the new building began on 23 February 1971.
facts.quote: Construction of the new building started on 23 February 1971.

facts.fact: The station was inaugurated on 6 September 1974.
facts.quote: In a ceremony attended by the country's elite, the station was inaugurated on 6 September 1974, with Zhivkov, the country's de facto ruler being present to cut the ribbon.

facts.fact: It was among 30 buildings built or renewed for the 30th anniversary of the 1944 coup.
facts.quote: The railway station was chosen to be one of 30 buildings that would be renovated, rebuilt or constructed as part of the 30 year celebration since the 1944 Bulgarian coup d'état.

facts.fact: It was completely renovated in 2016.
facts.quote: It was completely renovated in 2016.

facts.fact: Kuala Lumpur railway station was begun in 1910 and fully completed in 1917.
facts.quote: Construction began in 1910 and was fully completed in 1917.

facts.fact: It was the city's rail hub until Kuala Lumpur Sentral took over much of its role in 2001.
facts.quote: Replacing an older station on the same site, the station was Kuala Lumpur's railway hub in the city for the Federated Malay States Railways (FMSR) and its successor Keretapi Tanah Melayu (KTM) (English: Malayan Railways), before Kuala Lumpur Sentral station assumed much of its role in 2001.

facts.fact: Arthur Benison Hubback, assistant to the Director of Public Works, designed it in the region's Anglo-Asian style.
facts.quote: Arthur Benison Hubback, a British Architectural Assistant to the Director of Public Works, undertook the design of the station. He incorporated the unique Anglo-Asian architecture in the region on the station's design.

facts.fact: The main building mixes Western and Mughal forms, like Moorish Revival or Indo-Saracenic architecture.
facts.quote: The main structure, which contains a main hall, ticket counters, railway offices and the railway hotel, is primarily designed in a "Raj" styling, mixture of Western and Mughal similar to Moorish Revival or Indo-Saracenic architecture.

facts.fact: Horseshoe and ogee arches and large chhatris at the corners dominate the building, much like the nearby Sultan Abdul Samad Building.
facts.quote: Dominated by horseshoe and ogee arches, and large chhatris (six originally, with two added later) at the corners of the building accompanying smaller variations at the front, the station is comparable to its contemporaries like the Sultan Abdul Samad Building, surrounding structures constructed around the Merdeka Square and the Railway Administration Building directly across the street.

facts.fact: Its façade is fully plastered and painted in light colours, unlike similar buildings with exposed brick.
facts.quote: The façade of the station is completely plastered, as opposed to buildings of similar styles that opt for exposed brickwork, and painted in light colours (usually white or cream) throughout its service.

facts.fact: The platform roofs were first glazed and partly open to let steam-engine smoke escape.
facts.quote: The roofs were originally glazed, and were partially opened to allow smoke from steam locomotives to escape; corrugated roof sheets served as replacements later in the station's life.

facts.fact: It reopened as a railway museum on 31 August 2007.
facts.quote: The station was officially reopened on 31 August 2007 as a railway museum (where exhibitions are placed in the main hall and platform of the station), and was mooted to be converted into a cultural centre.

facts.fact: The Caferağa Medrese, next to Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, was built in 1559 by Mimar Sinan for Cafer Agha, under Suleiman the Magnificent.
facts.quote: It was built in 1559 by Mimar Sinan on the orders of Cafer Agha, during the reign of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566).

facts.fact: Sinan built it below the forecourt of the Hagia Sophia.
facts.quote: In 1559, he built the Cafer Ağa madrasah below the forecourt of the Hagia Sophia.

facts.fact: The main gate opens into an inner courtyard surrounded by the former teaching rooms.
facts.quote: The structure is entered through the main gate which leads into the inner courtyard, around which the former learning rooms are located.

facts.fact: In 1989 it became a centre where traditional Turkish crafts like calligraphy and ceramics are taught, made and sold.
facts.quote: The medrese was transformed by the Turkish Cultural Service Foundation in 1989 into a tourist centre with 15 classrooms/exhibition rooms, a big salon and a garden where traditional Turkish handicrafts such as calligraphy, ceramics, jewelry and so forth are taught, made and sold.

facts.fact: It lies within the Sultanahmet UNESCO World Heritage conservation area.
facts.quote: The medrese is located within the historical centre of Istanbul's Sultanhamet district, and as such comes within the UNESCO World Heritage Site conservation area which covers the entire district.

facts.fact: Terminal 3 opened in late 2004, replacing Terminal 1 as Israel's main international gateway.
facts.quote: Terminal 3 was inaugurated in late 2004, with Prime Minister Ariel Sharon speaking at the ceremony on 28 October, and opened to passengers the following month, replacing Terminal 1 as the main international gateway to and from Israel.

facts.fact: SOM designed the building; Moshe Safdie & Associates and TRA designed the linking structure and the airside areas and gates.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM). Moshe Safdie & Associates and TRA (now Black & Veatch) designed a linking structure and the airside departure areas and gates.

facts.fact: The design aimed to reflect how emotional arriving in and leaving Israel is.
facts.quote: The design was intended to reflect what its architects saw as the emotional character of arrival in and departure from Israel; Hamid Kia, the lead architect at SOM, contrasted air travel in the United States, where "not many people are greeted upon arrival", with Israel, where "departure or arrival is a very emotional experience".

facts.fact: Arriving and departing passengers share one connector and can see each other through glass, with views to the Judean Hills and a Seven Species garden.
facts.quote: Safdie's firm designed the connector between the landside and airside buildings so that arriving and departing passengers share a single volume and can see one another through a glass partition, with views towards the Judean Hills and a garden planted with the Seven Species.

facts.fact: An inverted dome under a white fabric ceiling diffuses daylight over departures; arrivals centres on a fountain.
facts.quote: The departures rotunda is covered by an inverted dome suspended above the concourse beneath a white fabric ceiling that diffuses daylight, while the arrivals hall is arranged around a central fountain, with tiered balconies and monumental columns.

facts.fact: Walls are clad in Jerusalem stone with white exposed concrete, glass and aluminium.
facts.quote: Vertical surfaces are clad in Jerusalem stone, used together with exposed white architectural concrete, glass and aluminium.

facts.fact: Concourses B, C and D opened with the terminal in 2004; concourse E was completed in 2018.
facts.quote: Concourses B, C, and D were opened when Terminal 3 opened in 2004, while concourse E was completed in 2018.

facts.fact: Bab Al Bahrain, "Gateway of Bahrain", stands in Manama's Customs Square and marks the main entrance to the Manama Souq.
facts.quote: Bab Al Bahrain (Arabic: باب البحرين, translitered Bāb al-Baḥrayn meaning Gateway of Bahrain) is a historical building located in the Customs Square in the central business district of Manama. It marks the main entrance to the Manama Souq.

facts.fact: It opened in 1949, designed by Charles Belgrave, the British adviser to the emir, and once stood on the coastline.
facts.quote: Opened in 1949 and designed by the British adviser to the emir, Charles Belgrave, Bab Al Bahrain once stood on the Manama coastline.

facts.fact: Land reclamation has left it several kilometres inland.
facts.quote: Due to extensive land reclamation in the later half of the 20th century, the structure is now several kilometres inland.

facts.fact: Its square is considered the region's first formal public space.
facts.quote: The square is considered to be the region's first formal public space.

facts.fact: It was refurbished in 1986 to add Islamic architectural features.
facts.quote: The monument itself was refurbished in 1986 to incorporate Islamic architectural features.

facts.fact: It is essentially a huge arch over a road, with two side arches for pedestrians.
facts.quote: Today the monument essentially consists of a huge arch, below which runs a road, which is often referred to as the entrance to the Manama souq (marketplace) and 2 sides arches are made for pedestrian.

facts.fact: Belgrave drove its creation at the entrance to the market, beside the old dhow landing jetties.
facts.quote: Belgrave understood the importance of trade and was the driving force behind the creation of the 'Bab Al Bahrain' (Gateway to Bahrain) structure at the entrance to the market area adjacent to the dhow landing jetties (now all reclaimed land).

facts.fact: Deira Clocktower is a roundabout monument in Deira, Dubai, giving access to the Al Maktoum Bridge.
facts.quote: Now a prominent monument in Deira, the roundabout provides access to the Al Maktoum Bridge, the first land crossing constructed between Deira and Bur Dubai.

facts.fact: It was built in 1965, designed by Otto Bullard and the Syrian architect Ziki Homsi.
facts.quote: The Clock Tower was built in 1965 and was designed by Otto Bullard and the Syrian architect Ziki Homsi, a partner at Architecture Design Construction (ADC) Office.

facts.fact: It was put up as a symbol of Dubai where the main routes into the city met.
facts.quote: It was erected as a symbol of Dubai and located in Deira because major routes into Dubai converged prior to the building of Dubai–Abu Dhabi Road.

facts.fact: In the early 1960s Shaikh Ahmed gave Shaikh Rashid a very large clock as a gift.
facts.quote: In the early 1960s Shaikh Ahmed gave Shaikh Rashid a clock as a gift. It was a very large clock.

facts.fact: According to an engineer of the time, its shape came from Bullard's own ideas and does not represent an oil drill bit.
facts.quote: The shape and design of the Clock Tower was from Mr Bulard’s own ideas and did not represent an Oil Drilling Bit or any other object.”

facts.fact: The Daily Telegraph listed it among the world's 17 most beautiful clock towers.
facts.quote: The Daily Telegraph newspaper listed the Dubai Clock Tower among the 17 of the world's most beautiful clock towers.

facts.fact: Moscow Cinema is a cinema on Charles Aznavour Square in Yerevan.
facts.quote: Moscow Cinema (Armenian: Մոսկվա կինոթատրոն, romanized: Moskva kinotatron) is a cinema hall in the Armenian capital Yerevan. It is located in Charles Aznavour Square on Abovyan Street.

facts.fact: It opened in 1936 on the site of the Saint Paul and Peter Church, demolished by the Soviet authorities.
facts.quote: The cinema was opened in 1936 on the site of Saint Paul and Peter Church, which was demolished in the 1930s by the Soviet authorities.

facts.fact: It was designed by Tiran Yerkanyan and Gevorg Kochar.
facts.quote: The building was designed by architects Tiran Yerkanyan and Gevorg Kochar.

facts.fact: In 1960 Gevorg Kochar and Telman Gevorkyan redesigned the building.
facts.quote: In 1960, the building was redesigned by architects Gevorg Kochar and Telman Gevorkyan.

facts.fact: In 1983 its façade was decorated with scenes from famous Soviet-Armenian films.
facts.quote: In 1983, the building was redeveloped when the facade was decorated with scenes of many famous Soviet-Armenian movies including Chapayev, Pepo, David Bek and Sayat Nova.

facts.fact: It is the main venue of the Golden Apricot Yerevan International Film Festival.
facts.quote: Moscow Cinema is the main venue of the Golden Apricot Yerevan International Film Festival, an international film festival held in Yerevan every year since 2004.

facts.fact: It has four halls, the largest seating 491, and an open-air theatre on its east side.
facts.quote: Currently, Moscow Cinema has 4 theatre halls: the red hall with 491 seats, the blue hall with 350 seats, the small red hall with 49 seats and the gallery with 35 seats. The cinema has also an open-air theatre located at the eastern side of the building.

facts.fact: The Tbilisi City Assembly Building is a clock-towered building on Freedom Square that houses the City Assembly.
facts.quote: Tbilisi City Assembly Building (Georgian: თბილისის საკრებულოს შენობა) is a clock-towered edifice situated in the southern side of Freedom Square (in Georgian - tavisuplebis moedani), Tbilisi, capital of Georgia. It houses the City Assembly (sakrebulo).

facts.fact: The original building dates from the 1830s, under Imperial Russian rule, and has been rebuilt several times.
facts.quote: The original building was built under the Imperial Russian rule in the 1830s but was reconstructed several times, taking a different look over the past two centuries.

facts.fact: Until 1879 it housed the chief of police and the police department.
facts.quote: It served, until 1879, as a Chancellery of Chief Policemaster and police department.

facts.fact: Paul Stern won the 1878 competition to remodel it as City Hall.
facts.quote: A competition announced in 1878 for the remodeling the building to the City Hall (Gorodskoy Dom) was won by the architect Paul Stern's project.

facts.fact: Its exterior follows the then-popular Exotic style with Neo-Moorish design.
facts.quote: It exterior architecture reflects the then-popular Exotic style with Neo-Moorish design.

facts.fact: The tower was added in 1910 and the building enlarged in 1912.
facts.quote: A tower was added in 1910 and the building was further enlarged in 1912.

facts.fact: The Basílica del Salvador stands in the Barrio Brasil of Santiago de Chile.
facts.quote: The Basílica del Salvador is a basilica located at the corner of Huérfanos Street and Almirante Barroso Street in the Barrio Brasil of Santiago de Chile.

facts.fact: It was designed by the German architect Teodoro Burchard in the Neo-Gothic style.
facts.quote: The basilica was designed by the German architect Teodoro Burchard in the Neo Gothic style.

facts.fact: Josué Smith Solar renovated it in 1932.
facts.quote: It was renovated by Josué Smith Solar in 1932.

facts.fact: Earthquakes in 1985 and 2010 badly damaged it.
facts.quote: Two earthquakes, one in 1985 and the other in 2010, badly damaged the basilica.

facts.fact: The cathedral stands on the site of Kiswarkancha, the Inca palace of Viracocha on Cusco's main square.
facts.quote: The Incas built the temple known as Kiswarkancha on the main square in Cusco. It was the Inca palace of Viracocha, ruler of the Kingdom of Cusco around a century before the Spanish colonists arrived.

facts.fact: Building started under Juan Miguel de Veramendi in 1560, followed by Juan Correa and others.
facts.quote: Its construction was entrusted to Juan Miguel de Veramendi in 1560, who was replaced one year later by Juan Correa who worked until 1564.

facts.fact: From 1615 Miguel Gutiérrez Sencio, an admirer of Juan de Herrera's sober style, led the work with Francisco Becerra, finishing it in 1654.
facts.quote: In 1615, Miguel Gutiérrez Sencio, an architect who followed Vitruvius and Giacomo Barozzi, and an admirer of the sober and pure style (Herrerian style) established by Juan de Herrera in El Escorial Monastery, took over the direction of the work, along with Francisco Becerra. Under their direction, the Cathedral of Cuzco was completed in 1654.

facts.fact: It is built of local stone, with red granite blocks reused from the Inca fortress of Sacsayhuamán.
facts.quote: The construction material was stone from nearby areas and red granite blocks were also reused from the fortress known as Sacsayhuamán.

facts.fact: After the 1650 earthquake the upper façade was changed and the towers lost a level, giving the building its solid, short-towered look.
facts.quote: This earthquake motivated the change of the planes of the façade in its upper part and the suppression of the third body in the towers, which is why there is too much volume in the body, leaving the towers short, giving the appearance of solidity to the building.

facts.fact: Its three naves are of equal height, as in the cathedrals of Lima and Jaén.
facts.quote: The three naves are of equal height, as in the cathedrals of Lima and Jaén.

facts.fact: Fourteen cruciform pillars set out its twenty-four rib vaults, the largest over the entrance and the crossing.
facts.quote: It has fourteen cruciform pillars that define the distribution of the twenty-four rib vaults, the largest being the entrance vault and the crossing.

facts.fact: It has a Renaissance façade and Baroque, late-Gothic and Plateresque interiors.
facts.quote: This cathedral possesses a Renaissance façade and Baroque, late-Gothic and Plateresque interiors.

facts.fact: As part of Cusco's historic centre, it lies in the UNESCO World Heritage Site declared in 1983.
facts.quote: Also, in 1983, being part of the historic center of the city of Cusco, it is part of the central zone declared by UNESCO as World Heritage Site.
